Your factory sent a certificate. Whose name is on it as the certifier?
A passing lab report won't fix what the certificate itself is missing.
On imports, the certifier is usually the importer of record.
The cert also needs the certifier's full address, email and phone, plus when and where it was made, among other fields.

Passing test report? That's not the same as a finished certificate.
A finished product certificate has its own required content: each applicable rule listed separately, the product, the certifier, a records contact, and when and where it was made and tested.
The test supports the certificate. It isn't the certificate.

Your factory says the wall-powered toy is certified. Certified to which rule?
Who it's made for decides the paperwork: children's products get a CPC, general-use products a GCC, when a CPSC rule applies.
Most toys for kids that run on 120-volt wall power fall under their own CPSC rule, 16 CFR part 1505 (video games are excluded).
That rule also sets what goes on the package: electrical ratings, required warnings, and the month and year it was made (or a date code).

Toys stuck on hold, and the certificate cites one rule?
A children's toy certificate (CPC) has to list every applicable rule separately, not just the toy standard.
16 CFR part 1250 makes the applicable parts of ASTM F963-23 mandatory for toys. A painted toy for kids usually also falls under the lead paint ban, 16 CFR 1303.
A toy for children under 3 also falls under the small parts rule, 16 CFR 1501.

For most imports, July 8, 2026 moved certificate data from a folder to the customs entry.
Under 16 CFR 1110.13(a)(1), the certifier of an imported product eFiles the certificate data elements in ACE when the entry is filed. On imports, that's usually the importer.
Those elements come from the certificate itself: the product ID, each rule, the test lab and date, a records contact and more.
Mail imports go a different route: the data goes into CPSC's Product Registry before arrival.
Check the certificate before the entry, not after.

The retailer won't set the item, and the launch date keeps slipping.
Under 16 CFR 1110.13(b), the certifier must furnish the finished product certificate to each distributor or retailer.
A lab report supports a certificate. It doesn't replace it, and it doesn't name a certifier.
Send the retailer the CPSC certificate itself, with every applicable rule listed.

A certificate only in Chinese is a gap, even if every test passed.
Under 16 CFR 1110.9(a), certificates must be in English, and eFiled certificates must be in English.
You can add another language, with the same content.
Ask the factory for the English version of the CPSC certificate before the next shipment.

Five products on one certificate? That's one of the quietest gaps in a CPSC file.
Under 16 CFR 1110.13(a), each finished product certificate must describe only one product.
Five products usually means five certificates, each with its own product identifier, like a SKU or UPC.
Check that each CPSC certificate, a children's product certificate or a GCC, names one product and its own identifier.

Coin battery inside? That's usually a rule your certificate has to list.
16 CFR part 1263 (Reese's Law) sets performance and labeling requirements for consumer products with button cell or coin batteries, to keep the batteries away from kids.
Exceptions exist, like toys that meet the battery rules in part 1250, and zinc-air cells.
The free CPSC Finder has a battery product family for this.

"The parts are certified" doesn't mean the finished toy is.
Under 16 CFR 1110.19, component part certificates are voluntary. A finished product certifier may rely on them to issue its own certificate.
Component certificates are not eFiled at entry. The finished product certificate is the one that's required (16 CFR 1110.5).
Keep both: the parts certificates and your own.

Water bead toys have had their own section of the toy rule since March 12, 2026.
16 CFR 1250.4 adds performance and labeling requirements for water bead toys and toys containing water beads, on top of the toy standard in 1250.2, including a size test for the beads.
A certificate written before that date may cite only 1250.2.
Check that each applicable section is listed.

A GCC on a kids' product is usually the wrong certificate.
Under 16 CFR 1200.2, a children's product is one designed or intended primarily for children 12 and under, judged by four factors: the label, the marketing, how buyers see it, and the age guidelines.
Children's products subject to a CPSC rule get a Children's Product Certificate (CPC), not a GCC.
The free CPSC Finder asks for the intended age group, for this reason.

"The factory keeps all that" is not a records plan.
Under 16 CFR 1110.17, certifiers keep certificates and the test records behind them for at least five years from the certificate creation date.
On imports, the certifier is usually the importer (16 CFR 1110.7(a)).
If the test records behind your children's product certificate live only with the factory, that's a gap worth closing.

If CBP asked for your certificate today, could you send it by tomorrow?
Under 16 CFR 1110.13(c), certifiers make certificates available immediately, meaning within 24 hours, when CPSC or CBP asks.
"Let me ask the factory" can take longer than that.
Keep the CPSC certificate and its records on file before a certificate request comes in.

Baby rattle on your list? There's a rule just for rattles.
Under 16 CFR 1510.3, no portion of a rattle may enter and penetrate to the full depth of the cavity in the test fixture, both before and after the use and abuse tests.
It's its own rule, so the certificate lists it separately (16 CFR 1110.11(a)(2)).

More rules on a certificate doesn't always mean more lab tests.
Under 16 CFR 1110.11(d), the certificate still lists each applicable rule separately. But certifiers aren't required to run the same third party test on a sample more than once when one rule references or fully incorporates another with the same requirement.
If a lab quote repeats the same test for overlapping rules, it's fair to ask why.
Ask before you pay twice.

Selling coin or button batteries on their own? Look at the package first.
16 CFR 1263.4 sets labeling rules for button cell and coin battery packaging: a warning label on the principal display panel (if space is tight, the icon there and the text on a secondary panel), in English, clearly visible and legible.
The signal word WARNING and the safety alert symbol are black on orange, unless only one color is present or that would hurt visibility.
